narrative: Your application was denied because the model estimated a 72.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is a high-risk estimate, not a certainty, but it means the decision treated bar-passage risk as outweighing the rest of your profile. The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the fourth decile, below the accepted-student average of about the sixth decile, and this pushed the prediction toward failure. The second strongest factor was your undergraduate GPA of 3.00, below the accepted-student average of 3.23, which also pushed toward failure. The third was your first-year class standing: fifth decile versus an accepted average of sixth decile, again adding to the failure risk. In other words, the denial was driven less by a single weakness than by a consistent pattern of academic indicators below the admitted class. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction. To move forward, ask admissions for specific feedback, focus on demonstrating stronger academic performance in any additional coursework, consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve it, and reapply only after you can show evidence that addresses the academic-risk pattern. You may also ask whether a conditional or supported admission pathway exists.
